item.content:encoded:
My friend Tessa and her husband Greg took the love languages quiz on their third anniversary.
Tessa got “Quality Time.” Greg got “Acts of Service.”
For a while, it was great. Greg stopped buying her flowers and started putting his phone away at dinner. Tessa stopped planning date nights and started doing his laundry.
Then, last spring, Tessa had a brutal week at work. She came home, collapsed on the couch, and cried.
Greg, trying very hard, said: “Want me to clean the kitchen?”
“I don’t want the kitchen cleaned,” she sobbed. “I want a hug.”
“But… hugs aren’t your language.”
She told me this story and laughed until she cried again. Then she asked me something I couldn’t answer at the time:
“Is the whole love language thing even real?”
It turns out psychologists had been asking the same question.
Where the Love Languages Came From
In 1992, pastor and counselor Gary Chapman published The 5 Love Languages. It became one of the best-selling relationship books ever.
The five: words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service, and physical touch.
The idea is simple and appealing. Everyone has one primary way they feel loved. Learn your partner’s language, speak it, and your relationship thrives.
And honestly? Part of it is lovely. It got millions of couples talking about what makes them feel cared for.
But it wasn’t built on research. It came from Chapman’s counseling experience. So eventually, scientists checked.
What the Research Actually Found
In 2024, relationship researchers Emily Impett, Haeyoung Gideon Park, and Amy Muise published a review of the scientific evidence on love languages.
Their conclusion was gentle but clear: the core assumptions didn’t hold up well.
Most people don’t have one dominant love language. When researchers measure it, people tend to value all five, often quite a lot.
And the evidence that couples are happier when they “match” or speak each other’s specific language was weak.
Instead, the researchers suggested a different metaphor.
Love isn’t a language you need to translate.
It’s more like a balanced diet.
You don’t just need protein. You need a bit of everything. Some days you need more of one thing than another, depending on what’s going on.
Tessa doesn’t only need quality time.
On a bad night, she needs a hug.
On a big day, she needs words.
Always, she needs all of it.
What Actually Makes People Feel Loved
Relationship scientists often point to something bigger than any single “language”: responsiveness. Feeling that your partner understands you, values you, and cares about what you need right now.
Not what a quiz said three years ago.
Right now.
- Ask, don’t assume. “What would help most tonight?” beats any personality result. Needs change with the day.
- Offer a little of everything. A kind word, a few minutes of undivided attention, a hand on the shoulder, a small favor. Variety is the point.
- Watch for the moment, not the category. Stress often calls for comfort. Good news often calls for celebration. Read the room.
- Use the quiz as a conversation starter, not a rulebook. It’s great for learning what your partner tends to appreciate. It’s not a reason to withhold a hug.
- Notice what they light up about. People often show you how they want to be loved by how they love others.
…
What Happened With Tessa and Greg
They still joke about “the kitchen incident.”
But Greg changed his approach. Now, when she walks in looking wrecked, he asks one question: “Fix it, hug it, or talk it?”
Most nights, she picks “hug it.” Sometimes all three. Occasionally, “fix it,” which usually means pizza.
“It’s not that the love languages were wrong,” Tessa told me. “It’s that I’m not just one thing.”
If You Take One Thing Away…
We think love means finding the one right language.
Research says it means paying attention to what someone needs today.
Love languages matter because they got us talking about how we feel cared for. But no quiz can replace actually asking.
Don’t speak one language.
Speak the moment.
Awareness always comes before change.
If this stirred something in you, that’s worth paying attention to.
Do you really have just one love language? Or do you need a little of everything?
I write more about the psychology of emotional safety, attraction, and modern relationships in my newsletter, Great Life for You.
You’re welcome to join if this resonated.
This space is for people who want depth over performance.

item.content:encoded:
Many readers may be familiar with Gary Chapman’s excellent 1992 book, The Five Love Languages: The Secret to Love That Lasts. While I had heard of the book, I didn’t read it until a few years ago.
If you don’t know Chapman’s five love languages, they include:
- Words of Affirmation
- Physical Touch
- Receiving Gifts
- Quality Time
- Acts of Service
My best friend Stacey recommended the book when John and I encountered a rocky patch – a common occurrence in most marriages. I’m grateful to her because it helped us back then and continues to help us now.
John and I enjoyed talked about and discovering our top love languages. Conveniently for us, Words of Affirmation are both number one. Acts of Service is number two for me, while Quality Time is John’s.
Recently, however, John and I have figured out there’s a sixth love language – well, at least for us. We would call it Cooking Meals. Now, you may argue cooking meals fits in the category of Acts of Service or even Receiving Gifts. But we feel it’s a whole other level.
We all must eat. But sometimes in this busy world, the thought of having to cook anything is overwhelming. Sure, we can turn to fast food, takeout, frozen dinners, etc. But of course, this comes at a cost, both financially and sometimes nutritionally.
I remember how I felt when people brought over homemade meals right after I gave birth to each of my two sons. This time of life was incredibly overwhelming, and to cross “dinner” off the list for a day was huge.
John and I genuinely enjoy planning and cooking meals for the people we love. We’re blessed to cook dinner every Sunday for our son Jonathon and his significant other, Olivia. It’s fun to brainstorm new ideas and see the look of joy on their faces when we present the meal.
Our kitchen is rather small, so working together takes some coordination. But cooking is a weekend tradition John and I love. And bonus – I’m a “clean as you go” cook. So, the kitchen ends up looking less like a war zone when we finally put dinner on the table.
This love language is what motivated me to join Lasagna Love years ago. While I no longer am in the program (since I’m always discovering people in my own city who need meals) I highly recommend the organization if Cooking Meals is one of your love languages. Check ‘em out at lasagnalove.org.
One new thing I enjoy doing is praying for the people who will eat the meal I create. I feel it adds an extra layer of love.
Hats off to Mr. Chapman for such a life-changing concept and book. May we all learn our own Love Languages and spread their joy to those around us.
Amy Shankland is an empty-nester, writer, and fundraising professional living in Noblesville with her husband John and two dogs. You can reach her via email at amys@greenavenue.info.

item.content:encoded:
A FORMER St Columba's High pupil who is now travelling the world after learning to love languages at school returned to the classroom to inspire a new generation.
Anna Gibson, 24, told a group of students how opportunities have opened up for her after falling in love with both French and Spanish in secondary.
She went on to study the languages at university and, after living in Spain and Paris for two years, she is now heading for the Pacific island of Tahiti to teach English.
Anna was invited to back to the Gourock school by Modern languages principal Emma Donnelly to share her experiences and demonstrate how modern languages can impact career opportunities.
The Wemyss Bay woman said: "I have no background in languages at home or anything. When I started secondary I thought I would go down the science and engineering route.
"But I loved learning languages, I learned Spanish first then French. It was my passion and I was so encouraged by Emma and the teachers here. They are so supportive.
"I decided to go for it and do languages at Glasgow University, my parents were supportive and just said do what you love.
"I have never looked back since. I loved uni, I took every opportunity that came my way.
"I ended up teaching in France, I worked in Spain and then I went to live in Paris was two years. I have never said no to any opportunity.
"I am now going to teach English in Tahiti. I never thought imagined this would be my life. It is a dream come true.
"I think it is so important that young people like me know the doors that can open for you if you learn and speak another language."
Anna said: "When you speak the language of a country you understand the culture and the mindset, it unlocks so much more."
Her experiences had a massive impact on the third year pupils who have chosen to study a language at national level.
In Inverclyde schools, modern languages are optional from third year onwards.
Many of the pupils listening to the talk said afterwards that, like Anna, they want to travel.
Among them Anna Nelis told the Tele: "I love Spanish and I really want to travel. I was really impressed listening to Anna."
Modern languages principal Ms Donnelly said: "It was wonderful to have Anna here. She is incredible and has taken every opportunity. Anna is the perfect example of what you can achieve with languages.
"I heard some of the pupils saying that they were re-evaluating their lives following her talk."
